findingDetails.alternativeExplanation: The intended trust model may treat every branch and linked worktree under a trusted Git common directory as trusted by the operator. Under that policy, the code is consistent with repository-level trust, though the security boundary is broader than branch-level trust.
findingDetails.case: A maintainer checks out an untrusted contributor branch in a linked worktree of a trusted clone and commits. The trust check sees the same Git common directory, leaves SOURCE_ROOT pointed at the checked-out tree, then sources that tree’s hook-flags.sh during the commit.
findingDetails.claim: The common-directory equality check is insufficient to establish that the hook scripts in the checked-out worktree are trusted, allowing branch-controlled shell code to execute at commit time.
findingDetails.counterevidenceSought: The check rejects a separate clone unless its local skilled.trustRepoHooks setting is true. In the selected hook code, I looked for a revision or branch-origin check and an immutable source for hook-flags.sh; neither appears in the trust-to-source path.
findingDetails.downgradeTrigger: Downgrade if the security contract explicitly accepts all branches and linked worktrees sharing a trusted common directory, and maintainers cannot be induced to commit from contributor-controlled branches without ordinary code review.
findingDetails.evidence: The gate treats equal common Git directories as trusted and only marks a repository untrusted when the common directories differ or the local opt-in is absent. It then sources hook-flags.sh from SOURCE_ROOT, which was selected from the current repository tree. A branch that changes that sourced file can execute shell code as the committing user.
findingDetails.recommendation: Bind trust to an immutable hook source or revision, or require an explicit local opt-in for branch-controlled worktree hook code. Add a scoped case for an untrusted linked-worktree branch.
findingDetails.scopeProof: This claim is limited to the scoped pre-commit trust gate and its immediate source operation at lines 43-61. No cross-consumer claim is made.
findingDetails.title: Shared Git common-directory trust admits branch-controlled hook code
findingDetails.userImpact: A contributor-controlled branch can run arbitrary commands with the maintainer’s local permissions when the maintainer commits from a linked worktree.

findingDetails.alternativeExplanation: The command text may be a compact diagnostic label rather than a copyable shell command, but it is formatted as a command next to each result.
findingDetails.case: A caller supplies a custom --prompt containing an embedded quote or shell expansion, then copies the reported probe command to reproduce a result.
findingDetails.claim: The report's probe command does not round-trip shell-sensitive custom prompt values.
findingDetails.counterevidenceSought: Checked whether the custom prompt is executed by the checker or only inserted into a display string; the child call receives argv and the report prints the display string.
findingDetails.downgradeTrigger: Remove this advisory if the report labels the string as illustrative and does not imply that it is a replay command.
findingDetails.evidence: The display command interpolates raw prompt text inside double quotes. The actual child call passes the prompt as an argv element, and report() prints the display string on both PASS and FAIL rows.
findingDetails.recommendation: Render the command from shell-escaped argv or label the text as a diagnostic description that is not safe to copy.
findingDetails.scopeProof: Direct inspection of the only prompt-bearing command display and its paired run() call shows this issue is local to the probe leg; the launched probe uses spawnSync argv.
findingDetails.title: Doctor probe output does not preserve custom prompts as a replayable command
findingDetails.userImpact: Shell parsing can change or expand the prompt in the displayed command, making a failed route harder to reproduce and diagnose.

findingDetails.alternativeExplanation: The standalone dash might be intended as positional title text. The phase spec says no caller passes a title beginning with a dash, while REQ-001 explicitly covers unmatched arguments beginning with a dash and contains no lone-dash exception.
findingDetails.case: A caller runs create.sh - Feature, where the standalone '-' is not a supported option.
findingDetails.claim: REQ-001's unknown-option contract misses the standalone dash because the shell pattern does not match a one-character token.
findingDetails.counterevidenceSought: Checked the existing --goal regression and --with-goal happy-path test, the declared no- -- end-of-options scope, and the parser's fall-through behavior. Those checks establish coverage for multi-character flags and valid options, but not the standalone dash.
findingDetails.downgradeTrigger: Downgrade or resolve if the interface contract explicitly exempts a standalone '-' from option syntax and the accepted title behavior is documented and tested.
findingDetails.evidence: The -?* case pattern requires at least one character after the dash. A lone '-' misses that branch, reaches the catch-all that appends it to ARGS, and becomes part of FEATURE_DESCRIPTION. REQ-001 requires any unmatched dash-leading argument to fail. The test covers --goal and --with-goal but has no single-dash case.
findingDetails.recommendation: Reject the exact token '-' as an unmatched option and add a regression case that confirms it exits 1 before creating a spec folder.
findingDetails.scopeProof: The parser branch at lines 351-358 establishes the single-token case; the scoped test at lines 59-79 verifies only the multi-character --goal refusal and valid --with-goal path.
findingDetails.title: A lone dash bypasses create.sh's unknown-option refusal
findingDetails.userImpact: The malformed option is treated as feature text instead of being refused, so the scaffolder can continue with an unintended title and path.
